name: American persimmon
habitat: Old fields, fencerows, roadsides, woodland edges and poor dry uplands from New England south to Florida and west to Texas and Kansas; fruit often hangs on bare branches after the leaves drop, which is when it is easiest to spot.
parts: Only fully ripe fruit — squishy-soft, deep orange, wrinkling, and usually already on the ground. Unripe persimmon is loaded with tannins and is fiercely astringent; eating a lot of unripe fruit is the documented cause of diospyrobezoars, hard tannin masses that can obstruct the stomach or bowel. Astringency goes with ripeness, not with cold: Purdue Extension states outright that the fruit does not have to experience a frost to ripen. Frost simply happens to arrive around the same time. Skin, cook, or pass the pulp through a food mill to remove the large flat seeds.
harvest: Gather windfalls — shaking or picking firm fruit off the tree just gets you astringent fruit and wastes it. Persimmon is a heavy autumn food for deer, foxes, raccoons and opossums, so clear only part of the drop under any one tree and come back on later visits rather than stripping it once.
